source.title: TensorCast: The Missing Tensor Management Layer in Large Language Model Infrastructure
source.summary: Modern LLM infrastructure increasingly manages tensors not only as computation data, but also as persistent states shared across distributed components. Existing systems optimize individual tensor management tasks, such as model weight loading, KV cache management, and checkpoint synchronization, by deeply integrating task-specific mechanisms with execution engines, networks, or storage backends. However, this specialization creates isolated silos that hinder the reuse and composition of tensor management strategies across evolving LLM workloads. In this paper, we identify tensor lifecycle management as a missing abstraction layer in LLM infrastructure and propose Tensor-as-a-Service (TaaS), which decouples tensor state management from computation logic. We design and build TensorCast, a distributed tensor management layer that provides first-class tensor abstractions, programmable lifecycle primitives, and a runtime that separates tensor management policies from execution mechanisms. This enables developers to write tensor management programs using TensorCast APIs while transparently leveraging distributed execution and data movement. We integrate TensorCast with vLLM and SGLang and evaluate it across diverse tensor lifecycle workloads, including model weight materialization, weight synchronization, KV cache management, and programmable request routing. Our results show that TensorCast achieves competitive performance with specialized tensor management systems while enabling new cross-component optimization policies. A programmable policy implemented with TensorCast improves median TTFT by up to 93.2% under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads.

previous_facts.title: TensorCast: The Missing Tensor Management Layer in Large Language Model Infrastructure
previous_facts.event_hint: arXiv preprint (2608.06007v1, 6 Aug 2026) proposing TensorCast / Tensor-as-a-Service (TaaS), a distributed tensor lifecycle management layer for LLM infrastructure, integrated with vLLM and SGLang.
previous_facts.problem: Existing LLM systems optimize individual tensor management tasks (weight loading, KV cache placement/transfer, checkpoint sync) by deeply coupling task-specific mechanisms with execution engines, networks, or storage backends, creating isolated silos that prevent reuse/composition and block cross-component optimizations such as jointly balancing instance load and KV cache locality.
previous_facts.mechanism: A Tensor-as-a-Service (TaaS) layer decouples tensor lifecycle management from computation: first-class tensor abstractions (system-owned Artifact, caller-leased tensors), programmable lifecycle primitives (identify/place/materialize/transform_into/coordinate), a distributed tensor pool plus lifecycle runtime that separates policies from execution mechanisms, and an instance adaptor that confines engine-specific import/export. Uses view() for rank-specific slicing/resharding and a userspace mTCP implementation with multipath transmission for non-RDMA KV transfer.

evidence.claim: TensorCast accelerates model weight synchronization by 1.14x to 2.63x versus the Default updater that retrieves full weights from JFS via file path.
evidence.baseline: Default SGLang updater (full model weights from JFS through a file path)
evidence.condition: 2-node cluster; each node 64 CPUs, 500 GB DRAM, 4 x H800 GPUs; RDMA disabled for TensorCast for fair comparison; models Qwen3-14B and Qwen3-32B; training-serving sync pattern (RL post-training).
evidence.source_locator: Section 6.2 'Model Weight Synchronization', Results paragraph (Fig. 7), PDF Page 12.

evidence.claim: For Qwen3-32B (TP=2) KV cache retrieval, with RDMA enabled TensorCast achieves TTFT reductions of 60% to 87.5% (2.5x to 8x speedup) comparable to Mooncake, and significantly outperforms Mooncake with RDMA disabled.
evidence.value: 60% to 87.5% TTFT reduction (2.5x-8x speedup) with RDMA
evidence.baseline: State-of-the-art Mooncake KV-centric integration in SGLang under identical settings
evidence.condition: N-node cluster; each node 64 CPU, 1 TB DRAM, 8 x H800 GPUs, 200 Gbps RDMA links; LongBench prompts (~16k and ~35k tokens); 100% cache hit rate stress test; TTFT reduction measured for N-1 instances relative to first instance.
evidence.source_locator: Section 6.3 'High-Cardinality Tensor Management', Results paragraph (Fig. 8a-8d), PDF Page 12-13.

evidence.claim: For Qwen3-235B-A22B (TP=8), TensorCast is comparable to Mooncake under RDMA and better without RDMA; TP=8 introduces 4x more concurrent KV page retrieval requests than TP=2, increasing contention and reducing TTFT improvements for both systems.
evidence.baseline: Mooncake KV storage backend in SGLang
evidence.condition: Same N-node H800 cluster; TP=8; 16k/35k token prompts; Fig. 9a-9d.

evidence.claim: A programmable request-routing policy implemented with TensorCast (cache-aware routing plus KV-cache-migrating load rebalancing) improves median TTFT by up to 93.2% under highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads.
evidence.baseline: Compared against Load-aware, Load-aware+Mooncake, and Cache-aware router policies (Fig. 10)
evidence.condition: Highly concurrent multi-turn agentic coding workloads; three LogNorm inter-turn delay presets (fast/medium/slow, Table 3); exact comparison cell and session count not restated in visible text.
evidence.source_locator: Abstract (PDF Page 1); Section 6.4 'Programmable Request Router' and Fig. 10/11 (PDF Page 13-14).

evidence.claim: Agent workload presets use LogNorm-sampled inter-turn delays: fast (median 8.2s, P95 22.0s), medium (median 20.1s, P95 75.0s), slow (median 60.3s, P95 311s), representing tight coding-agent loops, typical SWE agents, and long research/planning agents respectively.
evidence.condition: Synthetic LogNorm sampling within a session used to drive the §6.4 router evaluation.
evidence.source_locator: Table 3 'The three inter-turn delay presets used by the LogNorm sampling within a session', PDF Page 13.

previous_facts.evaluation_context: Hardware: 2-node and N-node clusters of H800 GPUs (4x or 8x per node), 64 CPUs, 500 GB-1 TB DRAM, 200 Gbps RDMA links. Baselines: Default JFS weight updater and Mooncake (SGLang KV backend). Models: Qwen3-14B, Qwen3-32B, Qwen3-235B-A22B with TP=2 and TP=8. Datasets/workloads: LongBench prompts (~16k/35k tokens), 100% cache-hit KV-reuse stress test, and simulated multi-turn agent sessions (LogNorm inter-turn delays). Integrations: vLLM and SGLang. Reported metrics are TTFT reduction ratios and weight-sync speedups; cache hit rate vs session count also reported.
previous_facts.limitations: Evaluations cover inference workloads only; training-framework integration (Megatron-LM, DeepSpeed) is explicitly left as future work (Discussion, PDF Page 14). Authors explicitly disclaim that a general abstraction is inherently faster than every specialized implementation; under RDMA, TensorCast is only comparable (not superior) to Mooncake, with its advantage concentrated in the non-RDMA and composability cases. The headline 93.2% TTFT gain is conditioned on highly concurrent multi-turn agent workloads and a specific programmable policy; the exact comparison baseline and session count are not restated in the visible text. Agent workloads use synthetic LogNorm-sampled delays rather than a production trace. This is an arXiv v1 preprint.
previous_facts.project_relevance: Relevant to the KV-cache-aware network/scheduling question: TensorCast provides a composable layer where request routing, KV placement, and instance load can be jointly programmed, and it reports TTFT reductions and a 93.2% median-TTFT agent-workload gain. However, the visible evidence reports reduction ratios rather than absolute TPOT, token throughput, end-to-end P95, or network utilization, and the network-side value is mainly in the non-RDMA (mTCP multipath) and cross-component composition cases rather than beating specialized RDMA KV systems head-to-head. Treat as a systems/preprint signal on composability, pending absolute tail metrics and training-side validation.
